JSON: Name: cdw_noise_suppression_pipeline Title: Phenomenological nonlinear transport and noise analysis of sliding charge-density-wave nanowires to demonstrate suppression of low-frequency current fluctuations below the normal-electron limit Short Hypothesis: In quasi-one-dimensional, fully-gapped charge-density-wave nanowires, when the applied bias exceeds the depinning threshold and transport is dominated by the sliding Frohlich condensate, the normalized low-frequency current noise spectral density S_I/I^2 decreases with increasing current following a power-law S_I/I^2 ∝ I^{-γ} (γ>0) and can fall below the normalized noise level of thermalized single electrons in a passive resistor. Related Work: Conventional low-frequency electronic systems (metals, semiconductors, MOSFET channels) exhibit 1/f noise with a normalized spectral density S_I/I^2 that is approximately independent of current; deviations have been treated within phenomenological Hooge- and McWhorter-type models. Charge-density-wave (CDW) materials have been studied for broadband noise, Lorentzian bulges near depinning, and threshold-related excess noise; those studies primarily focused on threshold dynamics and often reported return to normal-electron noise at high bias. Prior CDW noise work lacked a compact nonlinear phenomenological framework that: (i) separates normal and collective current contributions over a wide bias range, (ii) includes threshold-voltage fluctuation terms, and (iii) quantitatively predicts noise scaling with current in the sliding regime. Existing experimental datasets are limited in device geometry diversity, material polymorph coverage, temperature ranges, and concurrent thermal/heating diagnostics, which leaves unresolved whether intrinsic sliding-condensate noise can be below the normal-electron limit and under which material or device conditions. Abstract: We propose an experimental and modeling pipeline to verify whether sliding charge-density-wave (CDW) condensates can produce current with normalized low-frequency noise below the limit set by thermalized single electrons. The approach combines fabrication of quasi-1D fully-gapped CDW nanowires, broadband current-noise spectroscopy across depinning and sliding regimes, in situ thermal diagnostics, and a constrained nonlinear phenomenological noise model that includes normal-conduction, CDW-conduction, and threshold-voltage fluctuation terms. The main contribution is a reproducible experimental protocol and quantitative fitting workflow to (1) separate normal and collective current contributions, (2) extract noise amplitudes associated with each channel, and (3) test scaling laws of the normalized noise versus current. Expected outcomes are (a) verification or falsification of inverse scaling S_I/I^2 ∝ I^{-γ} in the sliding regime, (b) estimates of intrinsic sliding-condensate noise amplitudes, and (c) benchmarking of CDW nanowires against conventional channels for low-frequency-noise-limited applications. Experiments: Materials and samples: fabricate and characterize at least N=6 devices per material (TaSe4_2I and NbS2-II polymorph) with channel widths W ∈ {50, 150, 350} nm, thickness d ∈ {50, 83, 120} nm, and lengths L ∈ {2, 5, 12} μm; include control devices: (i) patterned normal metal resistors of matched geometry and (ii) Si MOSFET channel simulations with identical channel area using McWhorter parameters. Transport and temperature ranges: measure I–V, differential conductance G(V), and four-probe resistance from T=120 K to 400 K to span below and above Peierls transitions; identify depinning threshold V_t at each T. Noise spectroscopy: for each device record voltage and current noise spectra S_V(f) and S_I(f) using a dynamic signal analyzer and a low-noise preamplifier in frequency band f=0.1 Hz–10 kHz, with primary reference metric at f_ref=10 Hz; measure at bias points sampling regions: (I) V<V_t (normal), (II) near V_t (depinning), (III) onset sliding, (IV) high-bias sliding up to device limit (V_max≈1.5V or I_max limited by heating). Heating controls: perform in-situ Raman thermometry and COMSOL steady-state thermal simulations at representative bias points to quantify ΔT and exclude Joule heating as dominant noise source. Data extraction and model fitting: compute normalized noise S_I/I^2(f_ref), fit S_I/I^2 vs I to power-law S_I/I^2 ∝ I^{-γ}; fit nonlinear phenomenological model parameters {hδG^2/G^2, hδΓ^2/Γ^2, hδV^2/V^2, a} to full spectra and I–V curves using constrained nonlinear least-squares; report confidence intervals and goodness-of-fit (R^2, reduced χ^2). Baselines and comparisons: compare measured S_I/I^2 to (a) matched normal-metal resistor, (b) McWhorter-model MOSFET noise estimate for same channel area, and (c) measurements above T_Peierls (CDW suppressed) on same devices. Ablations and controls: (1) temperature ablation: measure at T>T_Peierls to remove CDW contribution; (2) defect density ablation: introduce controlled disorder (ion irradiation or chemical) to vary pinning and repeat noise characterization; (3) contact/geometry ablation: vary contact metals and perform four-probe vs two-probe to isolate contact noise. Statistical analysis: report per-condition mean and standard error for S_I/I^2 and γ; require reproducible suppression below normal-electron baseline in ≥4/6 devices per material for positive confirmation. Risk Factors and Limitations: Sample and materials variability: high device-to-device variance in crystal quality, thickness, and pinning disorder may prevent reproducible observation of sliding-dominated transport and noise suppression. Pinning and defects: extrinsic pinning centers can dominate threshold fluctuations and mask intrinsic condensate noise; controlled disorder may alter phenomenology nonlinearly. Measurement floor and instrumentation: instrument noise floor, amplifier nonlinearities, and external electromagnetic interference may limit sensitivity and produce artifacts when claiming suppression below the thermal/normal-electron limit. Joule heating and thermal gradients: underestimated local heating can alter CDW state and mimic noise reduction; Raman and simulation checks have limited spatial resolution. Model identifiability and parameter degeneracy: nonlinear phenomenological model contains correlated parameters (hδG^2/G^2, hδΓ^2/Γ^2, hδV^2/V^2, a) that may not be uniquely identifiable from available data, leading to non-unique fits. Scalability and generalization: results obtained for quasi-1D fully-gapped CDWs may not generalize to partially gapped or 2D CDWs, or to different polymorphs; practical device integration challenges (yield, stability, temperature dependence) may limit application. Thermal boundary uncertainties: interfacial thermal resistances and substrate coupling estimates can be inaccurate and affect heating assessments. Statistical power: limited sample counts increase false-negative risk for detecting the hypothesized scaling law.
